chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from one of our companions, who said:

A group of people came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and found a son of his who was sick. They saw concern and grief in him, and he would not remain at rest. He said, 'By Allah, if anything happens to him, we fear that we will see from him what we dislike.'

He said, 'They did not wait long before they heard the outcry upon him. Behold, he had come out to them with a cheerful face, in a state different from what he had been in before. They said to him, 'May Allah sacrifice us for you! We were afraid that, from what we saw of you, if it were to happen, we would see from you what would sadden us.'
So he said to them, 'We love to be healthy regarding those we love. But when the Command of Allah comes, we submit regarding what we love.'
ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Baqir demonstrate patience and submission to divine decree upon the death of his son?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia concept of 'naturalness' (tabi'iyyah) in the Imams, demonstrating that their emotional responses to loss are genuine human reactions rather than mere pretense, yet they are immediately followed by conscious spiritual submission. It contextualizes the recitation of 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' not just as a ritual, but as a profound psychological transition from personal attachment to divine acceptance, reinforcing the theological balance between feeling and faith.
